title: Alfred Wegener: The Jigsaw Puzzle of the Continents
source_book: Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane (The Origin of Continents and Oceans)
source_chapter: Chapter 2: The Continental Drift Hypothesis and Geodetic Evidence
authenticity_note: Directly derived from Alfred Wegener's 1915 monograph detailing the matching coastlines of South America and Africa, identical fossil deposits of Mesosaurus and Glossopteris, and glacial striations in tropical zones.
summary: In 1910, looking at a world map, German meteorologist Alfred Wegener noticed that South America and Africa fit together like giant jigsaw puzzle pieces. Gathering fossils, ancient rocks, and coal beds across vast oceans, he proposed 'Continental Drift'—the startling realization that continents were once a single supercontinent called Pangaea and are constantly in motion.
content:
In the winter of 1910, meteorologist and polar explorer Alfred Wegener stood before a large atlas in Marburg, Germany. He gazed intently at the Atlantic Ocean. The bulging coastline of Brazil seemed specifically designed to slot into the concave notch of the Gulf of Guinea on the west coast of Africa.

Most geologists of his day dismissed this as an amusing coincidence, believing that the continents were rigid, sunken land bridges having dissolved beneath the sea. But Wegener refused to accept coincidence without evidence. He scoured library archives and paleontological papers. What he uncovered took his breath away.

Identical fossils of *Mesosaurus*, a freshwater reptile incapable of swimming across thousands of miles of saltwater ocean, were discovered in matching rock layers of both eastern South America and southern Africa. Furthermore, fossils of the ancient fern *Glossopteris* were found in Antarctica, India, Australia, and South Africa—regions now thousands of leagues apart with vastly different climates. Even more striking, glacial scars carved into bedrock by ancient ice sheets matched seamlessly across modern-day tropical Brazil and equatorial Africa.

In 1912, Wegener delivered his historic lecture, published in his 1915 book *The Origin of Continents and Oceans*. He argued that 300 million years ago, all landmasses formed a colossal single supercontinent he named *Pangaea* (meaning 'All-Earth') surrounded by a global ocean called *Panthalassa*. Over geological epochs, Pangaea fractured, and the continents slowly drifted through the ocean floor like massive icebergs.

Traditional geologists mocked him, demanding: "What colossal engine could possibly push granite continents across the ocean basin?" Unable to identify the exact driving mechanism, Wegener died tragically in a blizzard on a Greenland expedition in 1930 without seeing his theory vindicated.

Decades later, sonar ocean mapping revealed the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and mantle convection currents, confirming plate tectonics. Wegener's bold vision had transformed humanity's understanding of our dynamic, living planet.
